subject: Accounting
title: Accrued Expenses
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Accrued Expenses.

hook.text: Employees worked all December but won't get paid until January 5th. December still owes them.

buildup.text: Accrued expenses are costs incurred but not yet paid—wages, interest, utilities.

discovery.text: An adjusting entry records the expense in December and creates a liability for the amount owed.

twist.text: Skip this and December's expenses look too low—inflating profit that isn't real.

climax.text: Accruals ensure that expenses appear in the period they belong to, not when cash finally moves.

punchline.text: You owe it now. Record it now. Pay it later.

quiz.question: What is an accrued expense?
options: A cost incurred but not yet paid
A cost that has been refunded

details.summary: Accrued expenses are costs a business has incurred but not yet paid. This topic explains how to record accruals for wages, interest, utilities, and taxes so that financial statements reflect the true cost of doing business in each period.
details.whyItMatters: Without accruals, financial statements would only show expenses when cash leaves the bank—painting an inaccurate picture of profitability and misleading decision-makers.
takeaways: Accrued expenses are recorded as liabilities because the obligation exists even without payment
Common accruals include wages earned but unpaid and interest accumulated but not yet due
Accrual entries are reversed when the actual payment is made in the next period

faq.question: What are accrued expenses in bookkeeping?
faq.answer: Accrued expenses are costs that have been incurred during an accounting period but haven't been paid yet. Examples include employee wages earned but not yet paid, interest accumulated on loans, and utility bills received after the period ends.

faq.question: Why do accrued expenses matter for accurate financial statements?
faq.answer: The matching principle requires expenses to be recorded in the period they are incurred, not when paid. Without accruals, a company could appear more profitable than it really is by simply delaying payments to the next reporting period.
